abstract: Changes in plasma Na+, K+ and Ca2+ levels are common in patients with chronic kidney disease or gastrointestinal disorders, or in those taking certain medications, and may promote atrial fibrillation or impair drug-induced cardioversion. Post-repolarisation refractoriness (PRR) is an established mechanism by which antiarrhythmic drugs suppress tachyarrhythmias. We investigated how changes in extracellular Na+, K+ and Ca2+ concentrations ([Na+]o, [K+]o, [Ca2+]o) modulate ionic currents and PRR in healthy and fibrotic human atrial tissue. We used a multi-scale computational framework comprising an isolated atrial myocyte, a one-dimensional atrial tissue strand, and a virtual cohort of 14 left atrial digital twins, combined with Gaussian process emulators and variance-based global sensitivity analysis. Changes in [K+]o strongly modulated PRR by altering the inward rectifier K+ current (IK1), shifting the resting potential and thereby regulating Na+-current availability. In contrast, [Na+]o had only a weak effect on PRR, mediated primarily through the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, and [Ca2+]o had a negligible effect. Tissue PRR was more sensitive to electrolyte changes than myocyte PRR, reflecting electrolyte-dependent alterations in the safety factor for action potential propagation. Changes in [K+]o also substantially affected arrhythmia vulnerability, increasing inducibility and prolonging rhythm disturbances. We conclude that extracellular K+ is the principal plasma electrolyte determinant of atrial PRR and arrhythmia burden, acting primarily through IK1. Monitoring and maintaining serum K+ within the normal range may be important for managing atrial arrhythmia risk.
